n: Ahab had seventy descendants (“sons” can include grandsons) living in Samaria under guardians. Jehu writes to the city’s leaders and the princes’ tutors.

f.g: a large royal family; seventy may be a round number for completeness.

n: Jehu’s letter is a challenge: you have the princes, chariots, a fortified city, and weapons.
Choose the best of Ahab’s sons, crown him, and fight for your dynasty—if you dare.
The leaders are terrified: two kings had already fallen before Jehu. How could they resist?
The palace steward, city governor, elders, and guardians surrender completely: “We are your servants.”

f.w: he that was over the house

n: Jehu’s second letter demands the heads of Ahab’s seventy sons by tomorrow. The wording is ambiguous—“heads” could mean leaders—perhaps so Jehu could later deny direct responsibility.

f.g: a deliberate double meaning: leaders or literal heads.

n: The nobles kill the seventy princes and send their heads to Jezreel in baskets—a horrifying display of how power corrupts.
Jehu orders the heads piled in two heaps at the city gate, a gruesome warning common in the ancient Near East.
Jehu addresses the people: “You are innocent. I killed my master—but who killed all these?” He shifts blame and shows that Samaria’s own leaders have joined his side.
He declares that none of the Lord’s word against Ahab’s house will fail. God’s word does not “fall to the ground.”

f.w: there shall fall unto the earth nothing
f.g: none of it will go unfulfilled.

n: Jehu kills everyone connected to Ahab in Jezreel—relatives, officials, friends, and priests. Later, the prophet Hosea condemns the excessive bloodshed of Jezreel.

f.w: until he left him none remaining

n: Jehu heads to Samaria, stopping at a place where shepherds sheared sheep.

f.g: possibly Beth-eked of the shepherds, a place name.

n: He meets forty-two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah, on their way to visit the royal family, unaware of the coup.
Jehu has them seized and killed at a pit or well. His purge reaches into Judah’s royal family, related to Ahab by marriage.
Jehu meets Jehonadab son of Rechab, founder of a strict group devoted to the Lord, and invites him into his chariot as an ally. Clasping hands sealed agreement.

f.g: founder of the Rechabites, known for strict loyalty to the Lord.

n: “Come and see my zeal for the LORD.” Jehu’s boast reveals mixed motives—real zeal against Baal, but also self-promotion.
In Samaria, Jehu kills the rest of Ahab’s family, fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy.
Jehu pretends to be an even more devoted Baal worshiper than Ahab.
He summons every prophet, priest, and worshiper of Baal to a great sacrifice, threatening death to any who stay away. The narrator reveals it is a trap.
A sacred assembly for Baal is proclaimed.
Baal worshipers come from all Israel and pack Baal’s temple in Samaria from wall to wall.
Jehu has the keeper of the wardrobe give out special robes to all the Baal worshipers—marking every one of them.
Jehu and Jehonadab enter and ensure no worshipers of the Lord are present.
Eighty soldiers are stationed outside with orders that no one escape, on pain of their own lives.
After the offering, Jehu orders the guards in, and they kill all the Baal worshipers. They then press into the inner shrine of the temple.

f.w: the city of the house of Baal
f.g: probably the inner sanctuary or citadel of the temple.

n: They bring out the sacred pillars of Baal and burn them.
They smash Baal’s pillar, tear down the temple, and turn it into a public latrine—the ultimate desecration.
With that, organized Baal worship—brought in by Ahab and Jezebel—is wiped out of Israel.
Yet Jehu kept Jeroboam’s golden calves at Bethel and Dan. His reform served his politics as much as his faith.
The Lord commends Jehu for carrying out the judgment on Ahab’s house and promises that his dynasty will last four generations—the longest in Israel’s history.

f.w: thy children of the fourth generation

n: But Jehu did not follow the Lord with all his heart. Obeying one command zealously does not replace wholehearted discipleship.
From this time the Lord began to “cut off” parts of Israel. Hazael of Aram seized Israelite territory, fulfilling Elisha’s tears.
All the land east of the Jordan—Gilead and Bashan, the territories of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh—was lost.

f.w: Aroer, which is by the river Arnon
f.g: the southern limit of Israel’s land east of the Jordan.

n: Jehu’s deeds are in Israel’s chronicles. An Assyrian monument, the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, shows Jehu (or his envoy) bowing and paying tribute—the only known contemporary image of an Israelite king.
Jehu dies and is buried in Samaria; his son Jehoahaz succeeds him.
Jehu reigned twenty-eight years (about 841–814 BC).
